lessons.title: ASTs and Intermediate Representations
concepts: The AST (abstract syntax tree) is the program's essential structure: it keeps meaning (x + 2*3 as +(x, *(2,3))) and discards syntax (parentheses, semicolons). Every analysis and transformation works on the AST, not the text.
Desugaring simplifies the AST: complex constructs rewrite to simpler ones (for-loops → while, async/await → state machines). Fewer core forms means the optimizer and backend handle less.

IRs (intermediate representations) sit between AST and machine code: SSA (static single assignment, one assignment per variable) makes data flow explicit for optimization; bytecode (JVM, CPython) is a portable IR executed by a VM.

Optimization passes transform the IR: constant folding, dead-code elimination, inlining, loop unrolling. Understanding IR explains why 'obvious' source changes sometimes don't affect performance — the optimizer already did it.

You meet ASTs directly more than you think: linters, formatters, transpilers, and IDE refactorings all parse to ASTs. Reading AST dumps is a practical debugging skill (python -m ast, clang -Xclang -ast-dump).

example.code:
import ast
tree = ast.parse('x = 1 + 2 * 3')
print(ast.dump(tree, indent=2))
# Assign(targets=[Name(id='x')], value=BinOp(left=1, op=Add(),
#   right=BinOp(left=2, op=Mult(), right=3)))  -- precedence in the tree!
example.walkthrough: Read the dump: where is the precedence encoded? Now predict the dump for 'x = (1 + 2) * 3' before running it — what changes?

pitfalls: Common trap: 'the compiler sees my code' — it sees the AST/IR; formatting and comments are long gone.
Common trap: fighting the optimizer — hand-'optimizing' what constant folding already does; profile first.
Common trap: AST vs parse tree confusion — parse trees keep every token; ASTs keep meaning. Tools use ASTs.
Common trap: assuming evaluation order — the IR may reorder; sequence points and memory models define what's guaranteed.

lessons.title: Type Systems: Static vs Dynamic
concepts: Static typing checks types at compile time: mismatches are errors before the program runs. The cost is annotation and rigidity; the payoff is machine-checked contracts and better tooling.

Dynamic typing checks at runtime: variables hold anything, errors surface when the bad operation executes. The cost is runtime failures and weaker IDE help; the payoff is flexibility and speed of writing.
Gradual typing (TypeScript, Python type hints) is the pragmatic middle: annotate the boundaries and critical paths, leave the rest dynamic. Types as documentation that the machine verifies.

Soundness vs completeness: a sound type system rejects some correct programs (annoying but safe); most real systems are unsound in corners (null, casts, any). Know where your system's holes are — that's where the bugs live.

Type inference fills in annotations automatically (Hindley-Milner and descendants): you write `let x = 5` and the compiler knows it's an int. Inference gives static safety with dynamic feel — the best of both when it works.

example.code:
Worked example — where the bug is caught
Static: f(x: int) called with a string → compile error, caught in the editor, zero production impact.
Dynamic: same call → runs fine until that line executes at 3am → page the on-call.
Gradual: annotate f's signature; the checker flags the call site; untyped internals stay flexible.
Takeaway: the question isn't 'which is better' but 'where do you want the error?'
example.walkthrough: Take one untyped function you wrote and add annotations to its signature only — what did the checker find?

pitfalls: Common trap: 'dynamic means no types' — values still have types; checking just happens later, at runtime, in production.
Common trap: any/abandonment — one `any` at a boundary poisons inference downstream; contain it.
Common trap: types as bureaucracy — annotations nobody reads; types should encode real invariants (non-empty strings, positive ints).
Common trap: 'static typing makes it correct' — types check types, not logic; tests still required.

lessons.title: Garbage Collection: How Memory Cleans Itself
concepts: GC automates deallocation: the collector finds unreachable objects and reclaims them. You trade manual control (and manual bugs: use-after-free, leaks) for pauses and runtime overhead.
Tracing collectors start from roots (stack, globals) and mark reachable objects; unmarked ones are swept. The mark phase must see a consistent heap — hence stop-the-world pauses in simple collectors.

Generational GC exploits the weak generational hypothesis: most objects die young. New objects go in the nursery (collected often, cheaply); survivors get promoted to older generations (collected rarely).

Reference counting frees immediately when the count hits zero (CPython) but can't handle cycles (A↔B keeps both alive) — that's why CPython adds a cycle detector. Counting also costs on every assignment.

GC tuning is about pause goals: throughput collectors pause longer but collect more per pause; low-latency collectors (ZGC, Shenandoah) pause briefly by doing most work concurrently. Match the collector to the latency requirement.

example.code:
Worked example — the nursery
Loop creates 1M short-lived objects. Generational GC: nursery fills, minor collection reclaims ~99% in milliseconds (most died young), survivors promote.
Non-generational: every collection scans the entire heap including long-lived objects — 10x the pause.
Takeaway: the generational hypothesis is why modern GCs are fast — design for it (short-lived temporaries are fine).
example.walkthrough: Check your runtime's GC stats (python: gc.get_stats(); java: -Xlog:gc) — which generation does most collecting?

pitfalls: Common trap: 'GC means no memory issues' — leaks via forgotten references (caches, listeners) are alive to the GC and grow forever.
Common trap: finalizers for cleanup — non-deterministic timing; use explicit close/context managers for resources.
Common trap: tuning without measuring — changing collectors on vibes; GC logs first, then decide.
Common trap: fighting the nursery — object pooling 'to help the GC' usually hurts generational collectors.

lessons.title: Interpreters, Compilers, and JITs
concepts: Interpreters execute the program directly (AST walking or bytecode loop): fast startup, slow execution. Compilers translate to machine code ahead of time: slow build, fast execution.
Bytecode VMs (JVM, CPython, V8's Ignition) split the difference: compile once to portable bytecode, interpret it anywhere. Portability and tooling win; raw speed loses to native code.

JITs compile hot code at runtime: start interpreting, profile, then compile the hot paths with profile-guided optimization (inline the actual types seen). JavaScript and Java live here — warmup matters.

Deoptimization is the JIT's safety net: if an assumption breaks (a new type appears), it falls back to the interpreter. That's why microbenchmarks lie — steady-state performance differs from first-call performance.
AOT (ahead-of-time) compilation skips the runtime compiler: instant startup, no warmup, but no profile-guided optimization either. Choose by constraint: startup latency → AOT; peak throughput → JIT.

example.code:
Worked example — the warmup curve
JS function called 1M times: first 1k calls interpreted (~slow), next 10k baseline-compiled, then optimized-compiled with inlining (~10x faster).
Benchmark that measures only the first 100 calls reports the interpreter; production sees the optimized tier.
Takeaway: 'how fast is it' depends on WHEN you ask — always warm up benchmarks.
example.walkthrough: Benchmark a hot loop with and without warmup — measure the difference and explain each tier.

pitfalls: Common trap: cold benchmarks — measuring the interpreter and blaming the language.
Common trap: 'compiled is always faster' — a JIT with profile data often beats AOT on real workloads.
Common trap: ignoring startup — JIT warmup in a 200ms serverless function means you never leave the interpreter.
Common trap: deopt blindness — performance cliffs when types change; profile under realistic type variation.

lessons.title: Threat Modeling: Think Like an Attacker
concepts: Threat modeling asks four questions: what are we building, what can go wrong, what will we do about it, did we do a good job? Asked early, it finds design flaws when they're cheap; asked late, it finds incidents.

Map trust boundaries: every place data crosses from untrusted to trusted (user input → server, server → database, service → service) is an attack surface. Draw the data flows; the boundaries are where the threats live.

STRIDE is the classic mnemonic: Spoofing, Tampering, Repudiation, Information disclosure, Denial of service, Elevation of privilege. Walk each data flow through all six — it's a checklist against blind spots.
Rank by risk: likelihood × impact. A theoretical crypto break matters less than the SQL injection in the login form. Threat modeling without prioritization produces a scary list and no action.

The output is decisions, not documents: 'we parameterize all queries,' 'admin actions require step-up auth,' 'PII is encrypted at rest with per-tenant keys.' If the model doesn't change the design, it was theater.

example.code:
Worked example — modeling a login form
Data flow: browser → web server → database.
STRIDE: Spoofing (credential stuffing) → rate limiting + MFA; Tampering (parameter tampering) → server-side validation; Information disclosure (verbose errors) → generic messages; Elevation (admin flag in cookie) → server-side session.
Takeaway: 10 minutes of STRIDE produced 4 concrete design decisions.
example.walkthrough: Threat-model one feature you built: draw the flows, run STRIDE, list the decisions.

pitfalls: Common trap: modeling after building — findings become 'accepted risks' instead of design changes; model at design time.
Common trap: attacker omniscience — assuming the attacker knows internals; also assume they know nothing and find the real paths.
Common trap: the scary list — 50 threats with no ranking; prioritize or nothing gets fixed.
Common trap: 'we have a firewall' — perimeter thinking; assume breach and model internal flows too.

lessons.title: Hashing, Salting, and Password Storage
concepts: Never store passwords — store the output of a password hashing function: bcrypt, scrypt, or Argon2. These are deliberately slow (hundreds of ms) so brute force is expensive; fast hashes (SHA-256) are the wrong tool.
Salting: a unique random salt per password, stored alongside the hash, defeats rainbow tables — precomputed hash dictionaries become useless because each password hashes differently.
Peppering (a secret salt in the app config, not the DB) adds defense in depth: a DB dump alone isn't enough to crack. It's a complement to salting, not a replacement.
Work factor: tune the cost parameter so hashing takes ~250-500ms on your hardware, and re-tune yearly. The work factor is what keeps the hash expensive as attackers' hardware improves.

Migration reality: if you inherit MD5/SHA-1 password hashes, don't mass-reset — wrap: bcrypt(md5(password)) with a flag, then upgrade to pure bcrypt at next login. Secure the legacy without punishing users.

example.code:
Worked example — cracking economics
8-char password, SHA-256 unsalted: a single GPU tries billions/sec → cracked in minutes; rainbow tables make it instant.
Same password, bcrypt(cost 12) + unique salt: ~250ms per guess → centuries per password; salts kill precomputation.
Takeaway: the algorithm choice IS the security — everything else is details.
example.walkthrough: Audit a project's auth code (or a tutorial's): what hash, what salt, what work factor? Write the findings.

pitfalls: Common trap: fast hashes for passwords — SHA-256(password) is barely better than plaintext against GPUs.
Common trap: one global salt — a single salt for all users is just a pepper with extra steps; salt per password.
Common trap: inventing your own crypto — 'SHA-256 applied 1000 times' is not bcrypt; use the standard algorithms.
Common trap: security questions as backup — 'mother's maiden name' is a second, weaker password; prefer reset flows.

lessons.title: Symmetric vs Asymmetric Crypto
concepts: Symmetric crypto (AES): one shared key encrypts and decrypts. Fast, simple — and the key distribution problem: how do both sides get the key without anyone else seeing it?
Asymmetric crypto (RSA, elliptic curves): a public key encrypts / verifies, a private key decrypts / signs. Solves key distribution — publish the public key freely — but ~1000x slower than symmetric.
Hybrid is how the real world works: asymmetric crypto exchanges a temporary symmetric session key (TLS handshake), then symmetric crypto carries the bulk data. Each does what it's good at.

Signatures vs encryption: encryption provides confidentiality (no one else can read); signatures provide authenticity and integrity (it came from the key holder, unmodified). Know which one your requirement needs — they're different tools.

The failure modes are never the math: they're key management (where are private keys stored?), randomness (predictable nonces/IVs), and protocol misuse (ECB mode, home-rolled padding). Crypto bugs live in the plumbing.

example.code:
Worked example — the TLS handshake, simplified
Client: 'let's talk' → Server: here's my certificate (public key, signed by a CA).
Client verifies the CA signature (authenticity), generates a session key, encrypts it with the server's public key.
Both sides: switch to AES with the session key for the bulk transfer.
Takeaway: asymmetric for trust establishment, symmetric for speed — the hybrid pattern.
example.walkthrough: Explain to a peer: why can't we just use RSA for everything? (Time the difference with openssl speed.)

pitfalls: Common trap: 'encrypted' = 'secure' — ECB-mode AES leaks patterns; encryption without integrity invites tampering; mode and protocol matter.
Common trap: home-rolled crypto — your custom cipher is breakable; the standard ones survived decades of attack.
Common trap: key storage as afterthought — the world's best algorithm with the private key in the repo is theater.
Common trap: confusing hashing with encryption — hashes are one-way; 'decrypting a hash' is brute force, not a feature.

lessons.title: Authentication vs Authorization
concepts: Authentication (authN): proving who you are — passwords, MFA, SSO, certificates. It answers 'who is this?' and nothing else.
Authorization (authZ): deciding what you're allowed to do — roles, permissions, ACLs, policies. It answers 'may they?' and depends on authN having already answered 'who?'

Confusing them is the classic bug: 'the user is logged in' (authN) treated as 'the user may access this record' (authZ). Every IDOR (insecure direct object reference) is this confusion — /invoices/1234 served to any authenticated user.

Authorize server-side, on every request: client-side checks (hidden buttons) are UX, not security. The API must re-verify ownership/role for the specific resource on each call — never trust the client's claims.

Sessions and tokens: session IDs must be random, rotated on privilege change, and invalidated on logout; JWTs must be validated (signature, expiry, audience) — an unsigned or never-expiring JWT is a forever-key.

example.code:
Worked example — the IDOR
GET /api/invoices/1234 with a valid session returns invoice 1234 — belonging to another customer.
Root cause: authN checked (logged in ✓), authZ skipped (is this YOUR invoice? ✗).
Fix: server-side check — invoice.customer_id == session.customer_id — on every request.
Takeaway: authentication without authorization is a locked front door with open windows.
example.walkthrough: Audit one API endpoint you use: is there a server-side ownership check on the resource ID?

pitfalls: Common trap: client-side authorization — hiding the admin button; the API still serves /admin to anyone who asks.
Common trap: authN as authZ — 'logged in' ≠ 'allowed'; check the specific permission on the specific resource.
Common trap: predictable session IDs — sequential or guessable tokens are account takeover; use cryptographic randomness.
Common trap: forever tokens — JWTs without expiry are unrevocable credentials; keep lifetimes short, rotate.

lessons.title: Common Vulnerability Classes: Injection, XSS, Overflows
concepts: Injection (SQL, command, LDAP): untrusted input interpreted as code. The fix is structural: parameterized queries / prepared statements separate code from data — never string-concatenate input into commands.

XSS (cross-site scripting): attacker script runs in victims' browsers via your pages. Stored XSS (in your DB, served to everyone) is the nightmare. Fix: output-encode by context, Content-Security-Policy headers, and frameworks that escape by default.

Buffer overflows: writing past a fixed buffer corrupts adjacent memory — historically the path to remote code execution. Modern defenses: memory-safe languages, stack canaries, ASLR, non-executable stacks. Defense in depth, not one fix.
The meta-lesson: these are all trust-boundary failures — untrusted data treated as trusted instructions. Parameterize, encode, validate at the boundary, and the classes shrink dramatically.

Validation strategy: allowlist over denylist (define what's permitted, not what's forbidden), validate server-side (client validation is UX), and validate at the trust boundary — every boundary, every time.

example.code:
# VULNERABLE: string concatenation
# query = "SELECT * FROM users WHERE name = '" + name + "'"  -- ' OR '1'='1
# FIXED: parameterized — data stays data
import sqlite3
conn = sqlite3.connect(':memory:')
cur = conn.execute("SELECT * FROM users WHERE name = ?", (name,))
# the ? placeholder means `name` can never become SQL
example.walkthrough: Explain why the placeholder defeats `' OR '1'='1`: what does the database do differently with the parameter versus the concatenated string?

pitfalls: Common trap: 'we validate client-side' — attackers don't use your client; server-side or it didn't happen.
Common trap: denylist filtering — blocking 'SELECT' while allowing 'SeLeCt'; allowlists define the safe set.
Common trap: 'internal only' — internal apps get exposed (VPN lapses, SSRF); treat every boundary as hostile.
Common trap: patching one injection — fixing the login form while the search box concatenates; audit every query.

lessons.title: Big-O: Reading Growth Rates
concepts: Big-O describes how runtime or memory grows as input grows — the shape of the curve, not the speed. O(n) doubles when input doubles; O(n²) quadruples; O(2ⁿ) explodes beyond any hardware.
Drop constants and lower terms: O(2n + 100) is O(n). Big-O is about scaling behavior — but remember constants matter in practice (an O(n) with a huge constant can lose to O(n log n) at real sizes).

Know the landmarks: O(1) hash lookup, O(log n) binary search / balanced tree, O(n) scan, O(n log n) comparison sort, O(n²) naive nested loops, O(2ⁿ) brute-force subsets. Recognize them on sight in code.
Best/average/worst differ: quicksort is O(n log n) average but O(n²) worst (sorted input + bad pivot); hash tables are O(1) average but O(n) worst (collision attack). Interviews probe the worst case.

Amortized analysis: some operations are occasionally expensive but cheap on average (dynamic array doubling is O(1) amortized). 'Occasionally slow' is fine when the average holds — know which guarantee you're getting.

example.walkthrough: Rewrite has_dupes in O(n) with a set, then argue the worst case: what input makes the set version degrade, and why is it still the right trade?

pitfalls: Common trap: 'O(n) is always fast enough' — n=10⁹ makes O(n) too slow; know your n.
Common trap: ignoring the worst case — 'average O(1)' hash tables under adversarial input are O(n); interviews ask about the attack.
Common trap: Big-O as the whole story — cache effects and constants decide real performance; O is the first filter, not the last.
Common trap: confusing n — O(n) in 'number of users' vs 'number of bits'; define n before analyzing.

lessons.title: Hash Tables: The Workhorse
concepts: Hash tables give average O(1) insert/lookup/delete: hash the key → index into buckets → handle collisions. Nearly every performance-critical lookup structure is a hash table underneath.
Collision strategies: chaining (linked lists per bucket — degrades gracefully) vs open addressing (probe for the next slot — cache-friendly, hates high load factors). Both work; know the trade.
Load factor (items/buckets) controls performance: resize (rehash) when it passes ~0.7. Resizing is O(n) but amortized O(1) per insert — the same doubling trick as dynamic arrays.

Hash flooding: adversarial keys that all collide turn your O(1) table into O(n) — a real DoS vector. Defenses: randomized hashing (SipHash), per-process seeds. Language runtimes learned this the hard way.

Choose the hash for the job: cryptographic hashes (SHA-256) for security, fast non-crypto hashes (xxHash, FNV) for tables. Never use a crypto hash where speed matters or a fast hash where attackers matter.

example.code:
from collections import Counter
words = ['apple','banana','apple','cherry','banana','apple']
counts = Counter(words)   # hash table underneath: O(n) total
print(counts.most_common(1))  # [('apple', 3)]
example.walkthrough: Explain why Counter is O(n) average: what does each word's insertion cost, and what pathological input would make it O(n²)?

pitfalls: Common trap: 'hash tables are O(1)' — average, not worst; adversarial or degenerate hashing degrades.
Common trap: mutable keys — mutating a key after insertion corrupts the table's invariants silently.
Common trap: iteration order dependence — hash order isn't sorted order; don't rely on it across runs.
Common trap: rolling your own — table sizing, probing, and hash quality are subtle; use the stdlib.

lessons.title: Trees and Heaps
concepts: Binary search trees keep keys sorted with O(log n) operations — when balanced. An unbalanced BST degrades to a linked list (O(n)); self-balancing variants (AVL, red-black) restore the guarantee via rotations.

Heaps are for extremes: a min-heap gives O(1) access to the minimum and O(log n) insert/extract. Top-K, schedulers, and Dijkstra's algorithm are heap applications — 'I need the biggest/smallest repeatedly' means heap.
Tries (prefix trees) index strings by prefix: autocomplete and IP routing. O(m) lookup where m is key length — independent of how many keys exist. Memory-heavy but unbeatable for prefix queries.

B-trees are the database tree: high fanout (hundreds of children) matches disk page sizes, keeping tree height tiny (3-4 levels for billions of rows). Your database index is almost certainly a B-tree variant.

The interview move: when you hear 'sorted + dynamic' think balanced BST; 'extreme element repeatedly' think heap; 'prefix search' think trie; 'on-disk index' think B-tree. Match the structure to the access pattern.

example.code:
import heapq
stream = [5, 1, 9, 3, 7, 2, 8]
# top-3 largest, streaming: O(n log k)
h = []
for x in stream:
    heapq.heappush(h, x)
    if len(h) > 3: heapq.heappop(h)
print(sorted(h, reverse=True))  # [9, 8, 7]
example.walkthrough: Why is this O(n log 3) and not O(n log n)? What changes if k grows to n/2 — when does full sort win?

pitfalls: Common trap: 'trees are O(log n)' — only balanced ones; always ask what keeps it balanced.
Common trap: heap for sorted output — heaps give extremes, not sorted order; repeated extract-min is O(n log n), same as sorting.
Common trap: BST for everything — hash tables beat trees for pure lookup; trees win when order matters.
Common trap: recursion depth — recursive tree code on skewed input blows the stack; know your tree's height.

lessons.title: Graphs: BFS, DFS, and Shortest Paths
concepts: Graphs model relationships: vertices + edges. Your first decision is representation — adjacency list (sparse graphs, most real ones) vs matrix (dense, O(1) edge checks).

BFS (breadth-first) explores level by level: it finds shortest paths in unweighted graphs and is the answer to 'fewest hops/steps.' DFS (depth-first) goes deep first: it's the answer to 'is there a path / topological order / connected components.'

Dijkstra's algorithm: shortest paths with non-negative weights — O((V+E) log V) with a heap. Negative weights need Bellman-Ford; negative cycles make 'shortest' undefined. Know which precondition each algorithm needs.
Topological sort orders a DAG so dependencies come first (build systems, course prerequisites). A cycle means no valid order exists — detecting the cycle IS the answer ('impossible').

The interview pattern: 'shortest/fewest' → BFS or Dijkstra; 'connected/reachable' → DFS/BFS; 'ordering with dependencies' → topo sort; 'all pairs' → Floyd-Warshall (and check whether you really need it). Name the algorithm from the question's nouns.

example.walkthrough: Trace it on a 5-node graph: why does the FIRST time we pop the goal guarantee the shortest path? What breaks with weighted edges?

pitfalls: Common trap: DFS for shortest path — DFS finds A path, not the shortest; unweighted shortest is BFS's job.
Common trap: Dijkstra with negative weights — silently wrong answers; check preconditions.
Common trap: forgetting visited — infinite loops on cyclic graphs; the seen set is not optional.
Common trap: recursion for deep graphs — Python's recursion limit vs a 10⁶-node chain; iterate or setrecursionlimit consciously.

lessons.title: Dynamic Programming: Overlapping Subproblems
concepts: DP solves problems with two properties: optimal substructure (the optimal solution contains optimal solutions to subproblems) and overlapping subproblems (the same subproblems recur — so memoize them).

The two implementations: top-down memoization (recursive + cache — intuitive, pays recursion overhead) and bottom-up tabulation (iterative table — efficient, harder to derive). Same complexity, different shape.

The recipe: (1) define the state (what varies?), (2) write the recurrence (how does the answer build from smaller states?), (3) set base cases, (4) decide computation order. If you can't write the recurrence, you don't have a DP solution yet.

Classic patterns: 0/1 knapsack (take-or-skip per item), longest common subsequence (match-or-skip per character), coin change (unbounded choice per amount). Recognize the pattern and the recurrence follows.
Space optimization: many DP tables only need the previous row (knapsack, edit distance) — O(n) space instead of O(n·m). Interviews love the follow-up 'can you do it in less space?'

example.walkthrough: Count how many times fib(3) would be computed without the cache (draw the recursion tree to fib(5)). Then convert it to bottom-up tabulation.

pitfalls: Common trap: DP without overlapping subproblems — divide-and-conquer problems (mergesort) don't need memoization; check the property first.
Common trap: state explosion — too many dimensions in the state; simplify the state definition before coding.
Common trap: recurrence before base cases — the recurrence is half the solution; base cases are the other half.
Common trap: premature space optimization — get the table right first, then compress; wrong compressed tables are undebuggable.

lessons.title: Pipelining and Superscalar Execution
concepts: Pipelining overlaps instruction stages (fetch, decode, execute, memory, writeback) like an assembly line: while one instruction executes, the next decodes. Throughput approaches one instruction per cycle even though each takes five.

Hazards stall the pipeline: data hazards (an instruction needs a result not yet computed), control hazards (branches — the next instruction is unknown until resolved), structural hazards (two instructions need the same unit).

Branch prediction fights control hazards: predict the branch direction and speculatively execute. Correct predictions cost nothing; mispredictions flush the pipeline (~15 cycles). Predictable branches are nearly free.
Superscalar execution goes wider: multiple pipelines in parallel, issuing 2-4+ instructions per cycle when they're independent. Out-of-order execution reorders instructions to keep all pipelines fed.

The programmer's view: write predictable branches and independent instruction streams where it matters (hot loops), but remember the hardware already does heroic work — profile before hand-optimizing.

example.walkthrough: Explain the mechanism: what does the pipeline do during a mispredicted branch, and why does sorted data avoid it? When would you NOT sort first?

pitfalls: Common trap: 'fewer instructions = faster' — pipelined CPI depends on hazards, not just count; dependent chains stall.
Common trap: unpredictable branches in hot loops — the 15-cycle flush dwarfs the comparison cost.
Common trap: assuming in-order execution — the CPU reorders; reason about dependencies, not program order.
Common trap: micro-optimizing cold code — pipeline effects only matter where the profiler says it's hot.

lessons.title: Caches: L1/L2/L3 and Coherence
concepts: The memory hierarchy exists because fast memory is small and big memory is slow: registers (~1 cycle), L1 (~4), L2 (~12), L3 (~40), RAM (~200+), SSD/disk (millions). Every level caches the one below.

Cache lines (~64 bytes) are the transfer unit: accessing one byte loads the whole line. Spatial locality (nearby data) and temporal locality (reused data) are what make caches work — your access pattern decides your speed.

Associativity and eviction: caches can't hold everything, so they evict (usually ~LRU). Conflict misses happen when too many hot addresses map to the same set — a real effect in tight loops over power-of-2 strides.

Cache coherence (MESI protocol): with multiple cores each having caches, the hardware keeps them consistent — a write by core 0 invalidates core 1's copy. Coherence is automatic but not free: ping-ponging a line between cores is slow (false sharing).
Practical rules: traverse arrays sequentially, keep hot data compact (struct-of-arrays for scanned fields), and pad per-thread data to cache-line boundaries to avoid false sharing.

example.walkthrough: Explain the ping-pong: why does core 0's write to `a` stall core 1's increment of `b`? What does the padding change in the coherence traffic?

pitfalls: Common trap: 'cache makes it fast' — only with locality; pointer-chasing linked lists defeat every cache level.
Common trap: ignoring line size — touching 1 byte per 64-byte line wastes 63/64 of memory bandwidth.
Common trap: false sharing blindness — adjacent per-thread counters look innocent and run 10x slow.
Common trap: measuring without warmup — cold caches punish the first run; steady state is what matters.

lessons.title: Instruction Sets: RISC vs CISC
concepts: ISA is the contract between software and hardware: the instructions, registers, and memory model the CPU exposes. x86-64 (CISC) and ARM/RISC-V (RISC) are the two families you'll meet.

CISC (x86): dense, complex instructions (one instruction can load, add, and store), variable-length encoding, fewer visible registers historically. Born when memory was precious and compilers were dumb.

RISC (ARM, RISC-V): simple fixed-length instructions, load/store architecture (only explicit loads/stores touch memory), many registers. Born for pipelining — simple instructions flow through pipelines cleanly.

The irony: modern x86 CPUs decode CISC instructions into RISC-like micro-ops internally. The ISA is the interface; the implementation underneath is its own beast — judge by measured performance, not philosophy.

What actually matters to you: calling conventions (how functions pass args — the ABI), memory ordering strength (x86 strong, ARM weaker — see the memory-model lesson), and vector extensions (SSE/AVX, NEON) for data-parallel hot loops.

example.code:
Worked example — the same add, two ISAs
x86-64:  add rax, [rbx]        ; one instruction: load, add, writeback
AArch64: ldr x1, [x0]           ; explicit load
         add x0, x0, x1         ; add (registers only)
         str x0, [x2]           ; explicit store
Takeaway: CISC density vs RISC explicitness — and the x86 chip cracks that one instruction into micro-ops resembling the ARM sequence.
example.walkthrough: Look up your machine's ISA (uname -m) and one calling-convention fact: how are the first 6 integer args passed?

pitfalls: Common trap: 'RISC is always faster' — modern implementations matter more than ISA philosophy; measure.
Common trap: ISA as identity — code in C/Python; the ISA affects the compiler and the ABI, rarely your logic.
Common trap: ignoring the ABI — mixing calling conventions (or forgetting the red zone) corrupts stacks mysteriously.
Common trap: 'assembly is dead' — reading disassembly is still the fastest way to understand what the optimizer did.

lessons.title: Scheduling: How the OS Shares the CPU
concepts: The scheduler multiplexes N runnable threads onto M cores: it picks who runs, for how long (timeslice/quantum), and what happens on wake/block. Every latency story involves the scheduler.

Goals conflict: throughput (finish the most work), latency (respond fast), fairness (no starvation). Desktop schedulers favor interactive latency; batch schedulers favor throughput; real-time schedulers favor deadlines.

Preemption: the OS forcibly takes the CPU back at quantum end (timer interrupt). Cooperative 'scheduling' (async tasks yielding) isn't scheduling at all — one greedy task starves the rest, which is why event loops must never block.

Priority and starvation: high-priority threads preempt low ones, but without aging (gradually boosting waiters), low-priority work starves. Priority inversion (low holds a lock the high-priority thread needs) needs priority inheritance to fix.
What you control: thread priorities (rarely), affinity (pinning threads to cores — for cache warmth and NUMA), and mostly: don't fight the scheduler — fewer runnable threads than cores usually wins.

example.code:
Worked example — the latency spike
Service: 200 runnable threads on 16 cores, p99 latency spikes.
Cause: oversubscription — the scheduler time-slices 200 threads across 16 cores; each thread waits ~12 quanta between runs.
Fix: thread pool of 32 → runnable threads ≈ cores, queue the rest; p99 drops 5x.
Takeaway: runnable-thread count is a first-class performance variable.
example.walkthrough: Check a running system: how many runnable threads vs cores? (top/htop load, or /proc/stat) — is anything oversubscribed?

pitfalls: Common trap: more threads = more speed — beyond core count, threads add scheduling overhead, not throughput.
Common trap: 'real-time' priority as a fix — raising priority starves others; fix the oversubscription instead.
Common trap: ignoring the scheduler in latency analysis — 'the code is fast' but p99 is slow: check run-queue latency.
Common trap: affinity as default — pinning helps cache warmth but hurts when load shifts; measure.

lessons.title: File Systems: Inodes and Journaling
concepts: A file system maps names to data: directories map names → inode numbers; inodes hold metadata (size, permissions, timestamps) and pointers to data blocks. The filename is not the file — the inode is.

Hard links: two names, one inode (same file, two directory entries). Symbolic links: a name pointing to another name (can dangle). Deleting a name removes a link; the data dies when the last link and last open handle go away.

Journaling: before changing the on-disk structures, the FS writes its intent to a journal. After a crash, it replays the journal — the FS is consistent without a full scan. That's why ext4/xfs recover in seconds.

The page cache: the OS caches file data in free RAM — reads after the first are memory-speed. This is why 'disk is slow' benchmarks lie on second runs, and why databases manage their own caching carefully.

Durability reality: write() returns when data hits the page cache, not the disk. fsync() forces it to stable storage. Databases that skip fsync on commit are fast and dishonest — know which yours does.

example.code:
# inodes in action
$ echo hello > a.txt && ln a.txt b.txt && ls -i a.txt b.txt
# same inode number: two names, one file
$ echo world >> b.txt && cat a.txt   # 'world' appears: same underlying data
$ rm a.txt && cat b.txt              # still there: data dies with the last link
example.walkthrough: Predict: after `ln -s a.txt c.txt; rm a.txt`, what does `cat c.txt` do? Why does the hard-link case differ?

pitfalls: Common trap: 'write() = durable' — it's page-cache-durable; power loss eats it without fsync.
Common trap: deleting open files — `rm` on a file a process holds: the name's gone, the disk space isn't (until close).
Common trap: df vs du confusion — df reads the FS, du sums names; deleted-but-open files explain the gap.
Common trap: small-file metadata storms — millions of tiny files exhaust inodes before bytes; check inode usage too.

lessons.title: Inter-Process Communication
concepts: Processes are isolated — that's the point — so they communicate through OS-mediated channels: pipes, sockets, shared memory, message queues, and signals. Each is a different point on the speed/structure trade-off.
Pipes: unidirectional byte streams between related processes (parent/child) — the shell's `|` operator. Simple, kernel-buffered, no random access. `a | b` is IPC you're already fluent in.
Sockets: bidirectional, work across machines (TCP/UDP) or locally (Unix domain sockets — faster, no network stack). Your microservices are socket IPC with extra steps.

Shared memory: the fastest — processes map the same physical pages. But now you need cross-process synchronization (named semaphores, mutexes in shared memory), and you've reintroduced every threading hazard across process boundaries.
Signals are notifications, not data channels: SIGTERM/SIGKILL/SIGHUP carry ~1 bit ('something happened'). They're asynchronous and lossy — use them for control ('reload config'), never for data.

example.code:
# pipes: the shell's IPC
$ seq 1 1000000 | grep '42' | wc -l
# three processes, two pipes, kernel-buffered streaming -- no temp files
# unix socket vs TCP: same API, but AF_UNIX skips the network stack
example.walkthrough: Trace the data: how many copies does a byte take from seq to grep? Where does the kernel buffer sit, and what happens when grep is slower than seq?

pitfalls: Common trap: signals for data — 'I'll send SIGUSR1 with the value' — signals carry no payload; use a real channel.
Common trap: pipe buffer deadlock — both sides writing full buffers while nobody reads: classic self-deadlock.
Common trap: shared memory without sync — the fastest IPC with the most ways to corrupt; name the lock per region.
Common trap: TCP for local IPC by default — Unix domain sockets skip the network stack; use them locally.

lessons.title: TCP Reliability: Sequence Numbers and ACKs
concepts: TCP turns IP's best-effort packets into a reliable byte stream with three mechanisms: sequence numbers (every byte numbered), acknowledgments (receiver confirms what arrived), retransmission (sender resends what's unacknowledged).

The handshake (SYN, SYN-ACK, ACK) isn't ceremony — it synchronizes initial sequence numbers and confirms both directions work before data flows. 'Why three packets to say hello' = agreeing on the numbering.
Flow control (receive window): the receiver advertises how much buffer space it has; the sender never exceeds it. This protects the receiver from being overwhelmed — speed matching, per connection.

Congestion control (slow start, congestion avoidance): the sender probes for network capacity, backing off on loss. This protects the network itself — the reason the internet doesn't collapse when everyone streams at once.

Failure modes to know: head-of-line blocking (one lost packet stalls the stream), half-open connections (one side died silently — hence keepalives), and the retransmission ambiguity (was it lost, or just slow?).

example.code:
Worked example — the lost packet
Sender: bytes 1-1000, 1001-2000, 2001-3000. Packet 2 lost.
Receiver: ACKs 1000 (got bytes 1-1000), then duplicate ACKs for 1000 as packets 3+ arrive out of order.
Sender: 3 duplicate ACKs → fast retransmit of 1001-2000 (no waiting for the full timeout).
Takeaway: duplicate ACKs are the receiver saying 'I'm stuck at 1000' — the protocol's repair signal.
example.walkthrough: Sketch the sequence/ACK exchange for a 3-packet transfer where packet 2 is lost — label every number.

pitfalls: Common trap: 'TCP guarantees delivery' — it guarantees detection and retry, not magic; a dead peer is eventually reported, not resurrected.
Common trap: confusing flow and congestion control — window = receiver capacity; congestion window = network capacity. Both apply.
Common trap: tiny writes — 1-byte sends become 41-byte packets (Nagle exists for a reason); buffer your writes.
Common trap: ignoring half-open — dead peers hold connections (and memory) until keepalive/timeout finds them.

lessons.title: Routing: How Packets Find Their Way
concepts: Routing is a distributed computation: routers exchange reachability info (BGP between networks, OSPF/IS-IS within) and each builds a forwarding table mapping destination prefixes to next hops.
Longest-prefix match: a packet to 10.1.2.3 matches both 10.0.0.0/8 and 10.1.2.0/24 — the router picks the most specific (/24). Specificity wins; that's how overrides work.

BGP is policy, not shortest-path: networks choose routes by business relationships (prefer customers, then peers, then providers) as much as by hop count. 'The internet routes around damage' — slowly, by policy.

Traceroute exploits TTL: send packets with TTL=1,2,3... and each expiring router sends back ICMP time-exceeded, revealing the path hop by hop. It's a hack on an error mechanism — elegant and occasionally lied to.
NAT breaks end-to-end: private addresses get rewritten at the boundary, which is why inbound connections need hole-punching and why IPv6's address abundance matters beyond 'more addresses.'

example.code:
Worked example — the /24 override
Table: 10.0.0.0/8 → router A; 10.1.2.0/24 → router B.
Packet to 10.1.2.99: matches both; longest-prefix picks /24 → router B.
Use case: steer one subnet's traffic differently (a migration, a scrubbing center) without touching the /8.
Takeaway: specificity is the routing system's override mechanism.
example.walkthrough: Given 0.0.0.0/0 → ISP and 192.168.0.0/16 → LAN, where does 192.168.5.5 go? Where does 8.8.8.8 go? Why?

pitfalls: Common trap: 'shortest path' thinking — BGP routes by policy; the fewest hops often lose to the cheapest relationship.
Common trap: traceroute as truth — load balancers and ICMP filtering make paths look weirder than they are.
Common trap: forgetting NAT state — NAT entries expire; idle connections die at the boundary, not the endpoints.
Common trap: /31 and /32 confusion — point-to-point links and host routes have their own rules; check the mask math.

lessons.title: HTTP and the Request Lifecycle
concepts: HTTP is a request/response protocol over (usually) TCP+TLS: client sends method + path + headers, server responds with status + headers + body. Stateless by design — state lives in cookies/sessions/tokens, not the protocol.

Methods have semantics: GET (safe, idempotent, cacheable), POST (unsafe, non-idempotent), PUT (idempotent replace), DELETE (idempotent remove), PATCH (partial). Respecting the semantics is what makes caching and retries safe.
Status codes are classes: 2xx success, 3xx redirection (follow Location), 4xx client error (don't retry as-is), 5xx server error (maybe retry). Retry logic keys off the class, not individual codes.

The TLS handshake precedes every HTTPS request (or resumes a session): certificate validation, key exchange, then encrypted HTTP. That handshake latency is why connection reuse (keep-alive) and session resumption matter.

Full lifecycle: DNS → TCP handshake → TLS handshake → HTTP request → server processing → response → (keep-alive?) close. Latency budgets split across these phases — measure per phase before optimizing.

example.code:
# see the lifecycle yourself
$ curl -w 'dns:%{time_namelookup} tcp:%{time_connect} tls:%{time_appconnect} ttfb:%{time_starttransfer}\n' -o /dev/null -s https://example.com
# each phase timed separately: now you know WHERE the latency lives
example.walkthrough: Run it against three sites: which phase dominates each? What would you fix first for the slowest one?

pitfalls: Common trap: GET with side effects — crawlers and prefetchers GET everything; mutating on GET corrupts data.
Common trap: retrying 4xx — 400/404 won't succeed on retry; only retry 5xx/429 (with backoff) and idempotent methods.
Common trap: ignoring keep-alive — new TCP+TLS per request multiplies handshake latency; reuse connections.
Common trap: status 200 with error body — lying status codes break every client, cache, and monitor; use the real codes.

lessons.title: Testing Strategy: The Pyramid
concepts: The test pyramid: many fast unit tests (base), fewer integration tests (middle), few end-to-end tests (top). The shape encodes economics — unit tests are cheap and precise; E2E tests are expensive and brittle.

Unit tests verify one unit in isolation (mocked dependencies): they're the bug localizers — when one fails, you know exactly where. Slow or flaky unit tests rot the suite; keep them under ~100ms each.
Integration tests verify components together (real DB, real queue): they catch the contract mismatches unit tests can't — serialization, SQL, config. Fewer, slower, and worth every minute.

E2E tests verify user journeys through the real system: the only tests that catch 'the button posts to the wrong endpoint.' Also the flakiest — reserve them for critical paths, and quarantine flakes immediately.

The inverted pyramid (mostly E2E) is the classic failure: slow suite, vague failures, developers stop running it. If your suite takes an hour and nobody runs it, you have no tests — you have a ritual.

example.code:
Worked example — the pyramid in practice
Checkout service: 200 unit tests (pricing logic, cart math — 3s), 30 integration tests (API + test DB — 4 min), 5 E2E (full purchase flow — 10 min).
A pricing bug: unit test fails in 3s, pointing at the exact function. An E2E-only suite would have said 'checkout broken' after 10 minutes.
Takeaway: the pyramid buys failure localization.
example.walkthrough: Classify your last 10 tests into the pyramid — what's the actual shape? What should move?

pitfalls: Common trap: the ice-cream cone — 500 E2E tests, 10 unit tests; slow, vague, eventually abandoned.
Common trap: testing implementation — tests coupled to internals break on every refactor; test behavior.
Common trap: flaky tolerance — one flaky test teaches the team to ignore red builds; quarantine or fix within the day.
Common trap: coverage as target — 100% coverage with assertion-free tests is a costume; cover behavior that matters.

lessons.title: CI/CD: The Deployment Pipeline
concepts: CI/CD is the path from commit to production: build → test → (staging) → deploy, automated and repeatable. The goal: every commit is production-ready, and releasing is boring.
Continuous integration: merge to main frequently (daily+), and let the pipeline verify each merge. Long-lived branches are merge-conflict futures — integrate small and often.

The pipeline stages: compile/lint (fast feedback), unit tests, build artifact (immutable — the same binary flows to prod), integration tests, deploy to staging, smoke tests, production deploy. Fail fast: cheap stages first.

Deployment strategies: rolling (gradual replacement), blue-green (two environments, switch traffic), canary (new version to a slice of traffic, watch metrics). Choose by blast-radius tolerance — canary for the risky ones.

The pipeline is production: a broken build blocks everyone, so treat CI as a first-class system — fast (<10 min ideally), reliable (no flakes), and owned (someone fixes red builds today, not 'eventually').

example.code:
Worked example — the boring release
Pipeline: lint+unit (3 min) → build image (2 min) → integration (5 min) → canary 5% (15 min bake, error-rate alarms) → full rollout.
A bad commit: canary alarms fire at 5% — automatic rollback, 5% of users saw elevated errors for 3 minutes.
Without the pipeline: the same commit ships to 100% on a Friday. Takeaway: the pipeline converts outages into incidents.
example.walkthrough: Map your current path from commit to prod: how many manual steps? What's the rollback story?

pitfalls: Common trap: the Friday deploy — shipping when nobody's around to fix it; deploy when the team is present.
Common trap: snowflake deploys — manual steps that 'only Alice knows'; automate or document, preferably automate.
Common trap: untested rollback — the rollback path fails exactly when needed; test it like the deploy.
Common trap: pipeline as suggestion — 'just this once' manual prod changes; the one time it matters, it diverges.

lessons.title: Code Review as Engineering Practice
concepts: Code review's real purposes, in order: knowledge sharing (the team learns the codebase), defect detection (a second pair of eyes), and consistency (the codebase stays coherent). 'Catching bugs' is second, not first.
Review the design, not just the diff: does this change belong here? Is the abstraction right? Diff-level nits (formatting) belong to the linter — human review is for judgment the tools can't make.

Author responsibilities: small diffs (<400 lines — review quality collapses above), clear description (what + why, not just what), and self-review first (read your own diff; you'll catch half the issues).

Reviewer responsibilities: timely (<24h — blocked authors context-switch), kind and specific ('consider X because Y' not 'this is wrong'), and approve-with-nits vs request-changes honestly (don't block on taste).
The review is a conversation, not a gate: the goal is shared understanding of the change. Rubber-stamp approvals and nit-war reviews both destroy the practice — calibrate as a team, explicitly.

example.code:
Worked example — the review that caught the race
Diff: adds a cache to the request path. Reviewer: 'What synchronizes the cache fills? Two concurrent misses will both fetch and both write.'
Author: adds singleflight (request coalescing) — the race the author hadn't considered.
Takeaway: the reviewer supplied the concurrency judgment the author lacked — knowledge sharing AND defect detection in one comment.
example.walkthrough: Self-review your last diff as a hostile reviewer: what would you flag? Fix it before requesting review.

pitfalls: Common trap: the 3,000-line review — nobody reviews it well; split the change or accept the risk explicitly.
Common trap: nit-blocking — requesting changes over formatting the linter should own; automate taste.
Common trap: review as hazing — 'prove you're worthy'; reviews teach, they don't initiate.
Common trap: LGTM culture — instant approvals train authors that review is theater; review like it matters.

lessons.title: Transactions and ACID in Practice
concepts: ACID: Atomicity (all-or-nothing), Consistency (valid state to valid state), Isolation (concurrent transactions don't see each other's partial work), Durability (committed = survived). The contract that makes databases trustworthy.

Atomicity in practice: the money transfer — debit A, credit B — must be one atomic unit. Without it, crashes create money (credited, never debited) or destroy it. BEGIN/COMMIT is the mechanism; the alternative is manual compensation logic.

Isolation levels are the performance dial: SERIALIZABLE (safest, slowest) → REPEATABLE READ → READ COMMITTED → READ UNCOMMITTED (fastest, sees everything). Each step down trades anomalies (dirty reads, phantoms) for throughput — choose consciously.

Durability costs fsyncs: a commit isn't durable until the WAL hits stable storage. 'Commit' without fsync is a promise the power company can break — which is why databases group-commit (batch fsyncs) instead of skipping them.

The distributed caveat: ACID is per-database. Across services, you need sagas (compensating transactions) — 'refund the charge' as the undo of 'charge the card.' Distributed atomicity doesn't exist; compensation does.

example.code:
Worked example — the phantom read
Isolation: READ COMMITTED. T1: SELECT COUNT(*) → 100. T2: INSERT a row, COMMIT. T1: SELECT COUNT(*) → 101.
Same transaction, different answers — the phantom. REPEATABLE READ (snapshot) would have held 100.
Takeaway: the isolation level IS the answer's meaning — know which one your queries run under.
example.walkthrough: Check your database's default isolation level right now — then name one anomaly it permits.

pitfalls: Common trap: assuming SERIALIZABLE — most defaults are READ COMMITTED; your 'transaction' sees more than you think.
Common trap: long transactions — holding locks across user think-time; keep transactions short and server-side.
Common trap: no-transaction multi-statement writes — three INSERTs without BEGIN are three independent commits; crash between them = partial state.
Common trap: distributed wishful thinking — expecting cross-service atomicity; design the saga instead.

lessons.title: Replication vs Sharding
concepts: Replication = copies: the same data on multiple nodes. It buys read scaling (spread reads across replicas) and availability (survive node loss) — but not write scaling or capacity; every node holds everything.

Sharding = partitions: different data on different nodes. It buys write scaling and capacity (the dataset exceeds one machine) — but queries spanning shards get complex, and rebalancing is an operation, not a feature.

Read replicas lag: async replication means replicas are milliseconds-to-seconds behind. 'Read your own write' breaks when the write goes to primary and the read hits a lagging replica — route carefully or use causal consistency.

Failover isn't free: promoting a replica takes detection time + promotion time + client redirection. Async replicas may have lost the last writes — the RPO (recovery point objective) is a business decision, not a technical detail.

The decision tree: need availability + read scale → replication. Need capacity + write scale → sharding. Need both → sharded clusters with per-shard replication (and the operational budget to run it).

example.code:
Worked example — the laggy profile update
User updates profile (writes to primary), refreshes (read routed to replica, 200ms lag) → sees the old profile → updates AGAIN → duplicate/conflicting writes.
Fix options: read-your-writes routing (sticky to primary after write), or synchronous replication for this table.
Takeaway: replication lag is a UX bug until you design for it.
example.walkthrough: For your app's hottest write-then-read flow: where does the read go, and what lag can it see?

pitfalls: Common trap: 'replicated' = 'scaled' — replicas don't add write capacity or storage; that's sharding's job.
Common trap: ignoring lag in UX — designing as if replicas were synchronous; the stale read always arrives eventually.
Common trap: untested failover — the promotion runbook fails at 3am; rehearse it like a deploy.
Common trap: sharding too early — sharding is a one-way door with operational cost; replicate until the data forces it.

lessons.title: Query Planning: How the Optimizer Thinks
concepts: The query planner turns SQL into an execution plan: which indexes to use, join order, scan vs seek. EXPLAIN is the window into its thinking — learn to read it before you tune anything.

Index selection: the planner estimates costs using table statistics. Stale statistics → wrong estimates → wrong plans. ANALYZE (or auto-vacuum/stats) isn't housekeeping — it's the optimizer's eyesight.

The usual villains: sequential scans on large tables (missing index), nested-loop joins on big inputs (hash/merge join wanted), and functions on indexed columns (WHERE lower(email) = ... defeats the index — index the expression instead).

Parameter sniffing: the plan is built for the first parameter values seen; later values with different selectivity get the wrong plan. The fix is usually recompile hints or plan guides — and recognizing the symptom (fast sometimes, slow others, same query).

The tuning order: (1) EXPLAIN the slow query, (2) fix the query (selectivity, joins), (3) add the right index, (4) update statistics, (5) consider schema/query redesign. Indexes are step 3, not step 1 — and every index taxes writes.

example.code:
-- read the plan before tuning
EXPLAIN ANALYZE SELECT * FROM orders WHERE customer_id = 42 AND status = 'open';
-- Seq Scan on orders (cost=...) rows=10M  <- the villain: 10M rows scanned
-- Fix: CREATE INDEX ON orders (customer_id, status);  -- composite, equality cols first
-- Re-run EXPLAIN: Index Scan, rows=37. Same query, 1000x faster.
example.walkthrough: Run EXPLAIN (not ANALYZE) on one of your slow queries: what node type is at the top, and what does its row estimate vs actual tell you?

pitfalls: Common trap: index-everything — each index slows writes and costs space; index the queries you have, not the ones you imagine.
Common trap: tuning without EXPLAIN — guessing at indexes; the plan tells you what the planner actually chose.
Common trap: leading-wildcard LIKE — '%foo' can't use a b-tree index; use trigram/full-text indexes instead.
Common trap: N+1 queries — the ORM's favorite: 1 query + N follow-ups; the plan shows 1 fast query hiding N round trips.

lessons.title: P vs NP: What Intractability Means
concepts: P: problems solvable in polynomial time (sorting, shortest path). NP: problems whose solutions are verifiable in polynomial time (given a tour, checking its length is easy). The question: does easy-to-verify imply easy-to-solve?

NP-complete: the hardest problems in NP — if any NP-complete problem has a polynomial solution, all of NP does (via reductions). SAT, traveling salesman, graph coloring: solve one fast, solve them all.

Practical meaning: when you recognize your problem as NP-complete (scheduling, packing, routing variants), stop hunting for the perfect polynomial algorithm — it probably doesn't exist. Switch strategies: approximation, heuristics, constraints, or smaller inputs.

Reductions are the tool: to show problem X is hard, reduce a known NP-complete problem to X (transform its instances into X's). 'My scheduler is NP-complete because graph coloring reduces to it' — that's the sentence that changes the project plan.

The interview use: 'this looks NP-hard, so I'd propose...' — naming intractability and pivoting to approximation/heuristics is senior-level judgment. The worst answer is grinding for the optimal algorithm that isn't coming.

example.code:
Worked example — the delivery routes
Requirement: optimal routes for 500 stops, computed in seconds.
Recognition: traveling salesman → NP-complete; exact optimum at 500 stops is infeasible.
Pivot: heuristic (nearest-neighbor + 2-opt local search) gives within ~5% of optimal in seconds.
Takeaway: naming the hardness class turned an impossible requirement into a shippable one.
example.walkthrough: Take one 'optimize everything' requirement you've seen: is the underlying problem NP-hard? What's the heuristic pivot?

pitfalls: Common trap: 'NP = non-polynomial' — NP is nondeterministic polynomial (verifiable); the name misleads everyone once.
Common trap: proving hardness by vibes — 'this seems hard' isn't a reduction; learn one canonical reduction deeply.
Common trap: approximation shame — 'but it's not optimal' — 5% off optimal in seconds beats optimal never.
Common trap: ignoring input size — NP-complete at n=20 is trivially brute-forced; hardness bites as n grows.

lessons.title: Finite Automata in Practice
concepts: Finite automata: the simplest computation model — states + transitions, no memory beyond the current state. Regular expressions, protocol parsers, and lexical analyzers are automata in work clothes.

DFA vs NFA: deterministic (one transition per symbol per state) vs nondeterministic (multiple possible). They're equivalent in power (subset construction converts NFA→DFA) but NFAs are exponentially more concise to write — which is why regex engines use them.
The pumping lemma draws the boundary: finite automata can't count arbitrarily (no matching parentheses, no aⁿbⁿ). When your 'regex' needs nesting, you've left regular languages — reach for a parser.

State machines are the applied form: TCP connection states, UI workflows, order lifecycles. Drawing the states and transitions finds the missing transitions (what happens on timeout in state X?) before they become bugs.
In interviews: 'design a parser for...' → think states; 'validate this format' → regex iff regular; 'match nested tags' → not regex, use a stack (that's context-free, one level up). Name the level.

example.code:
Worked example — the order lifecycle as states
States: PENDING → PAID → SHIPPED → DELIVERED; plus CANCELLED (from PENDING/PAID), REFUNDED (from DELIVERED).
The diagram immediately asks: can SHIPPED go to CANCELLED? (Business decision, now explicit.) What about PAID → ? (missing transition found.)
Takeaway: the state machine made implicit rules explicit — and found the gaps.
example.walkthrough: Draw the states for one workflow you own: list every transition, then hunt for the missing ones.

pitfalls: Common trap: regex for nested structure — matching parentheses/tags needs a stack; regex can't count.
Common trap: implicit states — 'status' strings scattered through code instead of one state machine; transitions hide.
Common trap: missing transitions — every state needs a defined behavior for every event (even if 'ignore'); undefined = bug.
Common trap: NFA/DFA confusion — backtracking regex engines (NFA-like) can catastrophically backtrack; know your engine.

lessons.title: Cryptographic Hash Properties
concepts: Cryptographic hashes (SHA-256, SHA-3) have three security properties: preimage resistance (given h, can't find m), second-preimage resistance (given m1, can't find m2 with same hash), collision resistance (can't find any two inputs with the same hash).

Collision resistance is the strong one — and the one that breaks: MD5 and SHA-1 are both collision-broken (researchers produce colliding inputs). 'But nobody will attack us' is not a security argument; migrate.

Hashes are not encryption: they're one-way and deterministic — the same input always gives the same output, which is why password storage needs salts (and slow hashes), and why 'hash the credit card' is still a breach.
Length extension and domain separation: naive constructions (SHA-256(key || message) as a MAC) have structural weaknesses — use HMAC for message authentication, not home-rolled hash combos.

Where hashes actually go: integrity checks (file downloads), commitments (reveal later), Merkle trees (blockchains, certificate transparency), and password storage (with salt + work factor — the slow-hash lesson). Match the property to the use.

example.code:
# collision-broken vs safe, and determinism
$ echo -n 'hello' | sha256sum   # always the same: determinism is the point...
$ echo -n 'hello' | sha256sum   # ...and why unsalted password hashes fall to rainbow tables
# MD5 is broken for collisions: never use it where an attacker picks inputs
example.walkthrough: Explain: why does determinism make unsalted hashes vulnerable to precomputation, and which of the three properties does a salt restore?

pitfalls: Common trap: 'hashed = safe' — unsalted fast hashes of passwords fall to rainbow tables in seconds.
Common trap: MD5/SHA-1 for security — collision-broken; fine for checksums against accidents, not attackers.
Common trap: hash as encryption — 'we encrypted it with SHA-256' is a category error; hashes don't decrypt.
Common trap: home-rolled MACs — SHA-256(key||msg) has length-extension issues; use HMAC.

lessons.title: Threads vs Processes: The Concurrency Menu
concepts: A process is an isolated execution environment: its own memory space, file descriptors, and at least one thread. Processes are heavyweight but safe — one crashing rarely takes down another.

A thread is a lightweight execution unit inside a process: threads share the process's memory, which makes communication cheap and data races possible. Threads are the default tool for parallel work on shared data.
Use processes for isolation and fault tolerance (a crashing worker shouldn't kill the server); use threads for fine-grained parallelism over shared memory (a parallel loop over an array).

Concurrency is about dealing with many things at once (overlapping I/O waits); parallelism is about doing many things at once (multiple cores computing). Threads give you both; async gives you concurrency without parallelism.
The cost model: thread creation is cheap (~microseconds, KBs of stack) versus process creation, but thousands of threads still drown in context-switch overhead — which is why thread pools exist.

example.walkthrough: Trace the interleaving: thread A loads counter, thread B loads counter, both increment their copies, both store. One increment is lost. Now explain why fork() can't have this bug.

pitfalls: Common trap: 'threads are always faster' — for I/O-bound work yes; for CPU-bound in some runtimes (GIL) threads don't parallelize at all.
Common trap: confusing concurrency with parallelism — overlapping waits is not the same as simultaneous computation.
Common trap: thread-per-request at scale — 10,000 threads means 10,000 stacks and scheduler meltdown; use pools or async.
Common trap: assuming shared memory is free — sharing is cheap to set up and expensive to get right (races, cache effects).

lessons.title: Locks, Mutexes, and the Deadlock Problem
concepts: A mutex (mutual exclusion lock) guarantees that only one thread holds it at a time: lock → critical section → unlock. It converts a data race into serialized access — correctness at the cost of parallelism.

Lock granularity is the central trade-off: coarse locks (one big lock) are simple but serialize everything; fine locks (per-bucket) parallelize better but are harder to get right. Start coarse, measure, then refine.
Deadlock needs four conditions simultaneously (Coffman): mutual exclusion, hold-and-wait, no preemption, circular wait. Break any one and deadlock is impossible — lock ordering breaks circular wait.
Lock ordering discipline: always acquire multiple locks in the same global order (e.g., by address or by ID). If every thread locks A-then-B, the cycle can never form.

Keep critical sections short and never call unknown code (callbacks, virtual functions) while holding a lock — the unknown code may try to acquire another lock, and now your ordering discipline has a hole.

example.walkthrough: Explain why ordering by address breaks the circular-wait condition: can thread 1 hold B while waiting for A if everyone acquires in address order? What breaks if a==b?

pitfalls: Common trap: locking too much — wrapping huge code regions in one lock 'to be safe' serializes the program back to single-threaded.
Common trap: forgetting unlock on error paths — every return between lock and unlock needs the unlock; prefer scoped/RAII guards.
Common trap: 'it never deadlocked in testing' — deadlocks need the unlucky interleaving; absence in testing proves nothing.
Common trap: recursive locking confusion — a non-recursive mutex locked twice by the same thread deadlocks itself.

lessons.title: Atomics and Lock-Free Basics
concepts: Atomic operations execute indivisibly as far as other threads are concerned: no interleaving can split them. A single atomic increment cannot lose updates the way counter++ can.
Compare-and-swap (CAS) is the universal atomic primitive: 'if memory holds expected, store new, report success.' Locks, lock-free structures, and allocators are all built on CAS loops.
Lock-free doesn't mean wait-free or fast — it means the system as a whole progresses even if a thread stalls. A CAS retry loop under heavy contention can spin badly; measure before assuming.

Memory ordering matters: atomics have ordering guarantees (acquire/release/seq-cst) that prevent the compiler and CPU from reordering operations across the atomic in ways that break your protocol. Default to sequential consistency until profiling says otherwise.

Rule of thumb: counters and flags → atomics; compound invariants across multiple variables → locks. Reaching for lock-free structures before a lock proves too slow is premature optimization with correctness risk.

example.walkthrough: Walk the contention case: two threads CAS simultaneously — one wins, the other's expected is stale, so it reloads and retries. Why does this guarantee no lost increments?

pitfalls: Common trap: 'atomic means fast' — contended atomics bounce cache lines between cores and can be slower than a lock.
Common trap: atomicity of the wrong thing — making each field atomic doesn't make the pair consistent; invariants need locks or careful protocols.
Common trap: ignoring memory ordering — on weak-memory hardware (ARM), missing acquire/release can reorder your protocol into a bug.
Common trap: lock-free data structures by hand — ABA problems and safe memory reclamation are expert territory; use proven libraries.

lessons.title: Async, Event Loops, and Non-Blocking I/O
concepts: Async I/O handles thousands of concurrent operations on few threads: instead of blocking a thread per connection, one event loop dispatches completions. It's concurrency without thread-per-connection overhead.
The trade: async code must never block the event loop. One blocking call (a slow disk read, a lock wait) stalls every connection on that loop — async demands non-blocking discipline everywhere.

Use async for I/O-bound fan-out (10k idle connections, crawlers, proxies); use threads for CPU-bound parallelism and for blocking APIs you can't rewrite. Many systems mix: async front, thread pool for compute.

Backpressure is the async survival skill: when producers outrun consumers, unbounded queues grow until the process dies. Every async pipeline needs bounded queues with a defined full-policy (drop, block, shed load).

Debugging async is harder: stack traces cross await boundaries, and 'which operation is stuck' needs loop instrumentation. Budget the observability up front — metrics per stage, not just at the edges.

example.code:
# async: 1000 concurrent fetches, one thread
import asyncio
async def fetch(url):
    reader, writer = await asyncio.open_connection('example.com', 80)
    writer.write(b'GET / HTTP/1.0\r\n\r\n')
    data = await reader.read()
    return len(data)
# asyncio.gather(*(fetch(u) for u in urls))  -- 1000 in flight, ~1 thread
example.walkthrough: Contrast with the thread-per-connection version: what resource does each blocked thread hold (stack + kernel state), and why does the event loop avoid it? Where would a blocking DNS call hurt?

pitfalls: Common trap: blocking the loop — one synchronous call stalls all connections; audit every await for hidden blocking.
Common trap: async for CPU work — async doesn't parallelize computation; CPU-bound tasks need threads/processes.
Common trap: unbounded queues — producer/consumer without backpressure is a memory leak with extra steps.
Common trap: 'async is always faster' — for low connection counts, thread-per-request is simpler and fast enough.

lessons.title: Data Races and the Memory Model
concepts: A data race: two threads access the same memory, at least one writes, with no synchronization between them. Data races are undefined behavior in C/C++ — the program can do literally anything, not just 'the wrong value.'

The memory model defines what reorderings the compiler and CPU may perform. Without synchronization, Thread A writing x=1 then flag=1 doesn't guarantee Thread B sees x=1 when it sees flag=1 — the writes can become visible out of order.

Synchronization establishes happens-before: a mutex unlock happens-before the next lock of that mutex; an atomic store-release happens-before a load-acquire that reads it. Reason about happens-before edges, not about timing.
Tools beat reasoning: thread sanitizers (TSan) detect races at runtime with modest slowdown. Run your concurrent tests under TSan in CI — human review misses interleavings that the sanitizer catches.

Design rule: make sharing explicit. Shared-mutable state is the hazard; prefer message passing (channels/queues) or immutable data, and where sharing is needed, name the lock that protects each field in a comment.

example.walkthrough: Explain the failure: which reordering (compiler or CPU) lets B see ready=1 with stale data? Why does release/acquire on `ready` fix it?

pitfalls: Common trap: 'it works on x86' — x86 has a strong memory model; ARM doesn't. Code that's accidentally correct on x86 races on ARM.
Common trap: volatile as synchronization — volatile prevents some compiler optimization but provides no atomicity or ordering.
Common trap: testing for races — races need the unlucky interleaving; passing tests prove nothing. Use TSan.
Common trap: double-checked locking without atomics — the classic 'optimization' that is broken without proper ordering.

import threading
class Acct:
    def __init__(self, i, bal):
        self.id = i; self.bal = bal; self.mu = threading.Lock()
A, B = Acct(1, 1000), Acct(2, 1000)
def transfer(a, b, amt):
    first, second = (a, b) if a.id < b.id else (b, a)  # global order: lower id first

[t.join() for t in ts]

simulations.title: The thrashing server
simulations.brief: A server crawls: every request is slow, the disk light is solid, and there's plenty of free RAM.

steps.symptom: The server is slow with free RAM but constant disk activity.
evidence:
$ free: 12 GB free
$ disk: solid activity
$ symptom: every request slow
options: Suspect thrashing: the working set exceeds RAM and the pager is swapping constantly — check swap activity
steps.explain: Free RAM plus solid disk plus universal slowness is the thrashing signature: the system spends its time paging instead of working.

steps.symptom: Confirmed: heavy swap in/out; the workload's working set exceeds physical RAM.
options: Reduce the working set (fewer workers, smaller caches) or add RAM — stop the paging, not the symptoms
steps.explain: Thrashing is fixed by fitting the working set in RAM — fewer hungry workers, smaller caches, or more memory. More swap just moves the pain.

options: Confirm swap activity is near zero and latency recovered
Confirm the disk light is off
steps.explain: Near-zero page-in/out plus normal latency is the recovery proof — the system works instead of paging.

simulations.debrief: Thrashing = working set bigger than RAM. The fix is fitting the work in memory, not adding swap or restarting. vmstat's si/so columns tell the truth.

simulations.title: Process or thread?
simulations.brief: Choose the concurrency unit for two designs.

steps.text: A web server handles 10k concurrent connections, mostly idle. Concurrency unit?

choices.label: Threads (or async tasks): shared memory, cheap context — idle connections don't each need an address space
choices.feedback: Right: 10k processes would drown in memory overhead; threads share the address space.

choices.label: One process per connection
choices.feedback: 10k processes means 10k address spaces — the overhead kills the design.

choices.label: One single-threaded loop, no concurrency
choices.feedback: A single loop blocks on the first slow client — concurrency is the requirement.

steps.text: An image renderer runs untrusted plugins that must not read each other's memory. Unit?

choices.label: Processes: separate address spaces isolate the untrusted plugins from each other
choices.feedback: Right: isolation needs separate address spaces — processes are the hardware-enforced boundary.

choices.label: Threads: faster
choices.feedback: Threads share memory by design — one malicious plugin reads everything.

simulations.debrief: Threads for cheap concurrency with shared memory; processes for isolation with separate address spaces. The trust boundary decides.

checklist: Get 7–8 hours of sleep the night before — fatigue destroys recall faster than any topic gap.
Bring valid government-issued photo ID and arrive at the test center 30 minutes early.
Eat a real meal beforehand; bring water and a light snack if the center allows them.
Read every question twice before scanning the answer choices.
Flag uncertain questions and move on — return with fresh eyes at the end.
Eliminate the obviously wrong answers first, then compare the survivors.
Budget your time: answer steadily and keep a 10–15 minute review buffer.
Re-run your weakest-domain drill until mastery is at least 80%.
For Computer Organization: restate the 'why' behind each scenario answer in your own words — if you can't explain it, you don't own it.
